name: INA169NA_3K
title: INA139 and INA169: high-side unipolar current shunt monitors with current output, SOT-23-5
summary: The INA139 and INA169 sense the small voltage across a high-side shunt and turn it into an output current of 1000 µA per volt of sense voltage; one resistor from OUT to ground sets the output voltage, so the voltage gain is RL / 1 kΩ. The supply V+ and the input common-mode voltage are independent: 2.7 V to 40 V on the INA139 and 2.7 V to 60 V on the INA169. Quiescent current is 60 µA typical. Both come in a 5-pin SOT-23 (DBV); the INA139 is specified from -40 °C to +125 °C and the INA169 from -40 °C to +85 °C.
key_figures: 1000 µA/V typ (990 to 1010 µA/V), VSENSE 10 mV to 150 mV
INA139 2.7 V to 40 V; INA169 2.7 V to 60 V
±0.2 mV typ; ±1.5 mV max (INA139), ±1 mV max (INA169)

notes: INA139 and INA169 differ in voltage range: 40 V for the INA139 against 60 V for the INA169 on supply and common mode, and in absolute maximum supply and common-mode voltage (60 V against 75 V).
Specified range: INA139 -40 °C to +125 °C, INA169 -40 °C to +85 °C; every orderable code carries an operating range of -40 to 125 °C.
Automotive-qualified (AEC-Q100) versions are sold as INA139-Q1 and INA169-Q1.

circuits.title: Typical application
circuits.description: High-side current sense. The load current IS flows from the VIN+ supply (up to 60 V) through shunt RS into the load. The INA1x9 sees the drop across RS on pins 3 and 4 and sources a current into RL; the output voltage is VO = IS × RS × RL / 1 kΩ. V+ is a separate supply pin.

circuits.title: Basic circuit connections
circuits.description: The same high-side connection drawn with the load supply VP (2.7 V to 40 V for the INA139, 60 V for the INA169) and the device supply V+ as two inputs; V+ may come from VP or from its own source. RL from OUT to ground sets the voltage gain: RL = 1 kΩ gives 1, 100 kΩ gives 100 (see the gain table). VO is taken across RL.
notes: VPLUS may be tied to VP or fed separately, 2.7 V ≤ V+ ≤ 40 V (60 V for the INA169).

circuits.title: Buffering the output to drive an ADC
circuits.description: An OPA340 wired as a voltage follower sits between OUT and the ADC, so the ADC input impedance ZIN no longer appears in parallel with RL and the gain stays RL / 1 kΩ.
notes: Supply pins of U1 and U2 are not shown in this circuit.

circuits.title: Output filter
circuits.description: A capacitor CL across RL makes a single-pole low-pass at f-3dB = 1 / (2π RL CL). RL is chosen first for gain, then CL for the corner.
notes: The V+ connection is not shown in this circuit.

circuits.title: Offsetting the output with a resistor divider
circuits.description: R1 from a reference VR and R2 to ground both connect to OUT. Gain is set by R1 || R2; at zero current the output sits at VR × R2 / (R1 + R2), so it follows VR.
notes: The V+ connection is not shown in this circuit.

circuits.title: Offsetting the output with a current source
circuits.description: A REF200 100 µA current source from V+ feeds the OUT node alongside the INA1x9 output current. Gain is set by RL; the zero-current offset is 100 µA × RL and does not depend on V+.
notes: I1 sources current from VPLUS into VO. The V+ pin of U1 is not shown in this circuit.

circuits.title: Bipolar current measurement
circuits.description: Two devices sense a ±1 A load current in a 1 Ω shunt with their inputs crossed, so one or the other conducts according to direction. Each output passes through a 1N4148 so the active device cannot drive current into the idle one, then through a 10 kΩ resistor into a shared 20 kΩ to ground: the voltage at Output is the magnitude, scaled 20 V/V. Across the two 10 kΩ resistors a difference develops at the inputs of a TLV3201 comparator, whose output Sign gives the direction.
notes: VBUS is a battery; ILOAD is a current sink from LOAD to ground.

circuits.title: Bipolar current measurement using a differential ADC input
circuits.description: Two devices across one shunt with crossed inputs, each with its own 25 kΩ RL, feed two inputs of an ADS7870 set for differential conversion. For one current direction one output carries the signal while the other stays at zero, so the sign of the reading gives the direction.
notes: U3's pins are named by function: two multiplexer inputs, the 5 V supply and ground.

circuits.title: Multiplexed measurement using a logic signal for power
circuits.description: Several INA169s, each on its own shunt, take their V+ from separate digital I/O lines of an ADS7870; driving one line high selects that device. Their outputs meet through 1N4148 diodes at one RL and one ADC input, and the diodes stop an active device's output current flowing into an unpowered one.
notes: U3's pins are named by function: digital I/O lines, a multiplexer input, the 5 V supply and ground.

operation.text: Inside are a high-voltage precision op amp, two thin-film input resistors of 1 kΩ (RG1 at VIN+, RG2 at VIN-) trimmed to absolute value, and an output transistor Q1. The op amp forces the shunt voltage across RG1, and the resulting current leaves through Q1 at OUT. One supply is enough, and the inputs may sit above V+.

Accurate measurement extends to 0.5 V differential, which gives 500 µA out. Up to 2 V differential does no harm. The input is unipolar: pin 3 (VIN+) must be the more positive. With pin 3 below pin 4 the output current is zero and the part is not damaged.

OUT stays accurate only within its compliance range, which the sense voltage, the supply and the input common-mode voltage all restrict: the ceiling is the lower of (V+) - 0.7 V - VSENSE and VIN- - 0.5 V.

A larger RL gives more gain and less bandwidth (440 kHz at 10 kΩ, 220 kHz at 20 kΩ). Capacitance on OUT also narrows bandwidth, so for the widest response it is kept small. A capacitor across RL may be added on purpose to filter; it does not make the output unstable.

A larger shunt improves accuracy at small currents because offset matters less; a smaller one loses less voltage in the supply line. Performance is best with 50 mV to 100 mV across RS at full scale; 500 mV is the most for accurate measurement.

operation.topic: Choosing RL and loading the output
operation.text: RL sets the full-scale output voltage; gain is RL / 1 kΩ. Because OUT has a very high output impedance, RL up to 100 kΩ keeps good accuracy. Whatever follows must have an input impedance much higher than RL. An ADC input that behaves as a resistor to ground can be counted as part of RL; a dynamic ADC input instead adds an uncertain load in parallel with RL, and a buffer amplifier such as the OPA340 removes it.

Unbuffered, the high output impedance working into the ADC input and sample-and-hold capacitance cannot settle within one conversion at 1 MSPS. With the buffer the S/H is driven from a low impedance and higher rates are possible. An RC low-pass may go between buffer and ADC: the capacitor supplies the charge the sampler draws, the resistor keeps the op amp stable against that capacitor; values depend on the op amp and ADC.

With a single supply the zero-current output can be lifted off ground. A divider R1 to VR and R2 to ground on OUT gives an offset that tracks VR (useful for centring on the supply). A REF200 100 µA source into OUT gives a fixed offset of 100 µA × RL, independent of V+.

The part measures one direction only; two devices with crossed inputs cover both. Diodes in each output keep the conducting device from feeding the idle one. Either a comparator across two series resistors gives the sign, or a differential ADC input reads polarity directly because one output is zero while the other carries the signal.
Each device can take its V+ from an ADC digital I/O line and is selected by switching that line on; diodes on the outputs block current from a powered device into unpowered ones.

The inputs measure correctly above V+: V+ can be 5 V with a load supply of up to 40 V (60 V on the INA169), though the output range is limited by the lower of the two. Placing 0.1 µF close to V+ is recommended, with more for noisy supplies. Bypassing is not needed for stability; it serves to reject noise from noisy or high-impedance supplies, placed close to the pins. Quiescent current is 60 µA typical, so V+ may be taken from either side of the shunt with little error.
Outside the specified supply range, common-mode range or output swing the behaviour is not defined and such use is not recommended.

Route VIN+ and VIN- straight to the shunt pads, as close to the shunt as possible, so no extra resistance appears in series with it. RL goes from OUT (pin 1) to ground; read the output directly across RL, which matters most at high current where load current in the ground return would add error. The example layout places RL by OUT, the 0.1 µF capacitor by V+, and a via to the ground plane at GND.
ESD protection on chip is limited: keep the leads shorted together or store the parts in conductive foam to protect the MOS gates.
